blocks.content: The why-dns-exists topic covered the motivation. This topic covers the actual mechanics: exactly what happens, step by step, in the handful of milliseconds between typing a domain name and your browser actually receiving the IP address it needs to connect to.

This process involves several different servers, each one playing a genuinely distinct role, cooperating in a very specific sequence. Once you see the full chain laid out clearly, the whole system stops feeling mysterious.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575333-255893798.png
1. Step One: Checking the Cache First
blocks.text: 1. Step One: Checking the Cache First

blocks.content: Before doing any real lookup work at all, your browser, and often your operating system too, first checks whether it already knows the answer from a recent previous lookup. If the domain was looked up recently, the cached answer is used immediately, with no network lookup needed at all. This caching mechanism is covered in its own full dedicated topic later in this module.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575333-852568891.png
blocks.alt: Step One: Checking the Cache First

blocks.content: 2. The Recursive Resolver: Doing the Legwork on Your Behalf
blocks.text: 2. The Recursive Resolver: Doing the Legwork on Your Behalf

blocks.content: If nothing useful is cached, your request goes to a recursive resolver, often run by your internet service provider, or a well known public option. This resolver takes on the entire job of tracking down the final answer, so your browser never has to talk to more than this one single server directly.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575333-718435070.png
blocks.alt: The Recursive Resolver: Doing the Legwork on Your Behalf

blocks.title: Why it is called recursive
blocks.content: The resolver does not just forward your question once and give up if it does not get an immediate answer, it keeps following the trail, asking one server after another, until it genuinely finds the actual answer, then hands that single final result back to you.
3. Step Two: Asking the Root Server
blocks.text: 3. Step Two: Asking the Root Server

blocks.content: The resolver first asks one of the internet root servers. A root server does not actually know the specific answer for example.com, but it does know exactly which servers are responsible for handling the .com portion of the request, and points the resolver there next.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575333-438889160.png
blocks.alt: Step Two: Asking the Root Server

blocks.content: 4. Step Three: Asking the TLD Server
blocks.text: 4. Step Three: Asking the TLD Server

blocks.content: The resolver next asks the TLD, top level domain, server responsible for .com addresses. This server still does not know the exact final IP address either, but it does know specifically which server is authoritative for example.com in particular, and points the resolver there next.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575333-34123279.png
blocks.alt: Step Three: Asking the TLD Server

blocks.content: 5. Step Four: Asking the Authoritative Server
blocks.text: 5. Step Four: Asking the Authoritative Server

blocks.content: Finally, the resolver asks the authoritative server for example.com specifically, and THIS server genuinely does know the answer. It responds with the actual IP address, which the resolver then finally returns back to your waiting browser.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575334-680979471.png
blocks.alt: Step Four: Asking the Authoritative Server

6. The Full Chain, Start to Finish
blocks.text: 6. The Full Chain, Start to Finish

blocks.content: Putting every step together in order makes the whole journey concrete: your browser asks the resolver, the resolver asks the root server which points it toward .com, the resolver asks the .com TLD server which points it toward the authoritative server for example.com specifically, the resolver asks that authoritative server and finally gets the real IP address, and the resolver returns that answer all the way back to your browser.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575586-110032288.png

7. A Real World Analogy

Asking for directions with no map at all captures this well. The first person you ask does not know the exact address, but tells you to head toward downtown. Once downtown, someone else does not know the exact address either, but tells you it is on Main Street. Once on Main Street, someone finally points you at the exact building. Each stage narrows the search until you arrive at the precise answer.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437575586-275105352.png

blocks.title: An honest note on speed
blocks.content: Despite involving several separate servers, this entire chain typically completes in well under a second, often just a few milliseconds, especially once caching, covered fully later in this module, kicks in and skips steps entirely.
8. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming your browser talks directly to the authoritative server itself, when it actually only ever talks to the recursive resolver, which does the multi step legwork on its behalf.","Assuming a root server or TLD server knows the final IP address directly, when each one only ever knows which server to ask NEXT, narrowing the search one step at a time.","The resolver checks its cache first, before doing any real network lookup at all.","Root servers point toward TLD servers, TLD servers point toward authoritative servers, and only the authoritative server has the real answer.","This entire multi step process typically completes remarkably fast, often in just milliseconds."]
items: Assuming your browser talks directly to the authoritative server itself, when it actually only ever talks to the recursive resolver, which does the multi step legwork on its behalf.
Assuming a root server or TLD server knows the final IP address directly, when each one only ever knows which server to ask NEXT, narrowing the search one step at a time.
The resolver checks its cache first, before doing any real network lookup at all.
Root servers point toward TLD servers, TLD servers point toward authoritative servers, and only the authoritative server has the real answer.
This entire multi step process typically completes remarkably fast, often in just milliseconds.
